title: Cash flow forecast template for UK businesses: Free download now
snippet: A cash flow forecast shows what money you expect to come in and go out of your business, so you can spot potential shortfalls earlier. Find out how to build and update one, and download our free UK cash flow forecast template to get started. The post Cash flow forecast template for UK businesses: Free download now appeared first on Sage Advice UK.
fullText:
Running a business means knowing what money is coming in and what’s going out, not just today but also in the weeks and months ahead.

A cash flow forecast gives you that visibility. For sole traders, freelancers, and growing SMEs, that’s often the difference between staying afloat and running into trouble.

Key takeaways

A cash flow forecast estimates the money you expect to come in and go out over a set period, so you can spot shortfalls before they happen.

Unlike a profit forecast, it tracks when cash actually moves through your bank account, which is why a profitable business can still run short.

Record income when it’s likely to arrive, not when you invoice, and only include confirmed work.

The free template has dedicated rows for VAT, PAYE and corporation tax. Use only the rows that apply to your business.

Most small businesses update their forecast monthly, or weekly if cash is tight or income is irregular.

Cash flow pressure remains a real issue for businesses. According to Coface’s 2025 UK Payment Survey, 90% of UK companies surveyed experienced late payments in the past year, and 44% said payment delays were becoming more frequent. Government-commissioned research published in July 2025 estimates that late payments contribute to around 14,000 UK business closures each year, the equivalent of around 38 every day.

A cash flow forecasting template won’t prevent every problem, but it gives you the information you need to spot a potential issue before it becomes a crisis.

This guide explains what a cash flow forecast is, why it matters, and how to use one. You can also download the free cash flow forecast template below and start filling it in straight away.

Here’s what we’ll cover in the article:

What is a cash flow forecast?

A cash flow forecast is a forward-looking document that estimates how much money you expect to come in and go out of your business over a set period. It predicts whether you’ll have enough cash to cover your costs at any given point, before you get there.

A forecast isn’t a record of what happened – it’s a projection of what’s likely to happen, based on what you know today about your income and outgoings. That’s what makes it useful.

Most small businesses will run a forecast covering anywhere from one month to 12 months ahead, and update it regularly as their circumstances change.

These two are often confused, and the difference matters.

A profit forecast looks at whether your business is making more money than it’s spending overall. It’s based on revenue earned and costs incurred, regardless of when the cash actually moves.

A cash flow forecast, or cash flow projection, looks at when money physically enters and leaves your bank account. A business can be profitable on paper and still run into serious trouble if customers pay late, a large tax bill lands at the wrong time, or costs fall in a month when income is thin.

A straightforward example: you complete a project in March and invoice for £5,000. Your profit forecast includes £5,000 in March. But if your client pays in May, your cash flow forecast won’t show that money until it actually arrives. In the meantime, you still have rent, wages, and supplier payments to cover. This is why profitable businesses can and do run into cash flow problems. Understanding how your cash flow forecasting works in practice is just as important as the numbers themselves.

Why cash flow forecasting is important for small businesses

Most financial problems don’t arrive without warning. They build up gradually, and a forecast gives you the chance to spot them early enough to do something about it.

Avoiding cash shortfalls

A shortfall happens when your outgoings exceed your available cash, even temporarily. For a small business, that can mean missing payroll, defaulting on a supplier payment, or being unable to take on new work because you can’t cover the upfront costs. Forecasting doesn’t prevent shortfalls, but it tells you they’re coming. That gives you time to act, whether that means chasing an outstanding invoice, negotiating later payment of a supplier’s bill, or exploring suitable funding options, where appropriate, and seeking professional advice if you’re unsure.

Planning for tax payments

Whether you need to pay VAT, PAYE, or corporation tax, and how much and when, depends on your business’s specific circumstances. Not every business will have all three obligations, and filing and payment timetables can differ. Where they apply, a decent forecast can help you estimate roughly when they’re due and how much they’ll be. The problem for many small businesses is that these payments aren’t built into day-to-day cash planning, so they land as a surprise.

The free cash flow forecast template includes dedicated rows for VAT to HMRC, PAYE to HMRC, and corporation tax, so these obligations sit alongside your other outgoings rather than being an afterthought. Use only the rows that apply to your business.

Managing growth

Growth costs money before it makes money. Taking on a new member of staff or investing in equipment requires cash upfront, often before the revenue from that investment comes through.

A forecast lets you test whether your cash position can support a decision before you commit to it. That isn’t a reason to avoid growth, but to time it better.

Making informed decisions

The quality of a business decision is only as good as the information behind it. If you’re weighing up a new supplier or preparing for a quieter month, a regularly updated forecast gives you a factual basis to work from.

How to use the cash flow forecast template

The cash flow projection template is straightforward to set up.

Enter your company name, choose your period type (weekly, fortnightly or monthly), set your start date, and enter the number of periods you want to forecast across. Then work through the income and expenditure rows, filling in what you expect for each period.

Here’s how to approach each section.

Estimate your cash coming in

Start with your income. The cash flow forecast template for Excel gives you customer or sales channel rows, which you can label however makes sense for your business. A freelancer might use them for different clients. A product business might split them by sales channel.

Also include:

Expected loan or funding receipts if you’re waiting on finance

Any tax refunds you’re anticipating

Other one-off receipts that will land in a specific period

If your payment terms are 30 days, build that delay into your forecast.

List your cash going out

Work through the expenditure rows and enter your expected outgoings for each period. The template covers the most common costs for UK businesses, including:

Staff and payroll

Supplier and contractor payments

PAYE, VAT, and corporation tax to HMRC

Rent, utilities, and office costs

Insurance, subscriptions, and professional fees

For tax rows, enter the amounts in the period they are actually due to leave your account, not the period they relate to.

Review your opening and closing balances

Once your income and expenditure amounts are in place, then the cash flow summary at the bottom does the work. Your opening balance for the first period is the only figure you enter manually.

From there, the template automatically calculates your net cash flow and closing balance for each period, carrying the closing balance forward as the opening balance for the next period.

A positive closing balance means you expect to have cash available. A negative closing balance is a warning sign that needs attention before that period arrives.

Update your forecast regularly

A forecast you fill in once and never revisit loses its value quickly. As actual figures come in, update your template to reflect what really happened and adjust your projections forward.

How often you update depends on your situation. A business with tight cash flow or irregular income may need to review weekly. For most small businesses, a monthly update is enough to stay on top of things.

Monitor forecasted cash flows against actual cash flows

Updating your forecast is only half the job. The other half is comparing what you projected against what actually happened.

Each time you close out a period, go back to your forecast and fill in the real figures alongside your estimates. If your actual income came in lower than expected, or a cost ran higher than planned, note it and adjust your projections going forward.

Over time, this habit makes your forecasts more accurate. You start to see patterns, and you can build those realities into your numbers rather than working from assumptions that don’t reflect how your business works.

Cash flow forecast example

To see how the forecast works in practice, here is a simple example using a sole trader who runs a small landscaping business.

Opening balance: £2,500

In May, the business has two confirmed jobs worth £1,800 and £1,200 respectively. Based on 14-day payment terms, both payments are expected to land within the month. Total expected income for May: £3,000.

Outgoings for the same period:

Supplier payments (plants, materials): £800

Fuel and travel: £150

Public liability insurance (monthly portion): £45

HMRC VAT payment due in May: £600

Other costs: £80

Total expected expenditure: £1,675

Net cash flow: £3,000 minus £1,675 = £1,325

Closing balance: £2,500 plus £1,325 = £3,825

On paper, May looks healthy. But now imagine the client with the £1,200 job pays 30 days late.

The income drops to £1,800 for the month, the expenditure stays the same, and the net cash inflow falls to £125. The closing balance drops to £2,625.

The forecast doesn’t change the situation, but it tells you about it before it happens. That’s the value of running the numbers in advance.

If you know in April that May could be tight, you could ask for a deposit upfront, chase receivables early, or make sure you have enough in reserve to cover it.

How often should you update a cash flow forecast?

There is no single right answer, and it depends on your business. The more variable your income and outgoings, the more frequently you need to review your numbers.

Weekly updates

Weekly works best if your cash position is tight, your income is irregular, or you’re in the early stages of trading. Reviewing every week gives you enough time to react if something looks off, whether that’s a payment that hasn’t arrived or an unexpected cost landing earlier than planned.

Monthly updates

For most small businesses, a monthly update is enough. You review what actually came in and went out during the month, update your projections for the periods ahead, and adjust for anything that has changed. It should become a routine part of closing out the month rather than a separate task.

Rolling forecasts

A rolling forecast means you always maintain a set window of visibility ahead, typically 12 months, moving forward as each period passes. Rather than forecasting to a fixed year-end and starting again, you add a new period each time one closes.

This approach suits businesses that are growing, planning investment, or operating in sectors where conditions change quickly. It takes more discipline to maintain, but it gives you a more accurate picture over time.

Common cash flow forecasting mistakes to avoid

Even if you forecast regularly, it’s easy to fall into habits that make your numbers less reliable. These are the ones you should watch out for.

Overestimating income

Overestimating income is one of the most common forecasting mistakes for small businesses, and often the most damaging. It’s easy to forecast based on what you hope will come in, rather than what you can realistically expect.

If you’re quoting for three projects but only one is confirmed, only the confirmed one belongs in your forecast.

The same applies to timing. If a client has 30-day payment terms, don’t record the income on the day you invoice. Record it when the money is likely to land in your account.

Forgetting VAT and tax bills

Where VAT, PAYE, and corporation tax apply to your business, they can still catch you off guard. They don’t feel like everyday expenses, and the cash to cover them has often been spent by the time the bill arrives.

The template includes dedicated rows for each of these tax costs. Use the rows that apply to your business. If you’re unsure how VAT works for your business, it’s worth getting clear on your obligations before they affect your cash position.

Not updating your forecast

A forecast built in January and left untouched through March is no longer a forecast. It’s a record of what you expected three months ago. As your circumstances change, your numbers should change with them.

Set a regular time each week or month to review and update. It doesn’t have to take long, but it has to happen consistently to be useful.

Ignoring seasonal changes

Most businesses have periods that are busier or quieter than others. If your forecast treats every month the same, it won’t reflect reality.

Build seasonal patterns into your projections from the start, even if your estimates are rough. You can refine them as you gather more data over time.

Using invoice dates instead of payment dates

This is a common oversight, particularly for small businesses new to forecasting. Your forecast should reflect when cash actually moves, not when you raise an invoice or receive a bill.

If you issue an invoice today on 30-day terms, that income belongs in next month’s forecast, not this one.

How accounting software takes the guesswork out of cash flow

A spreadsheet works well when your finances are straightforward. But as your business grows and transactions increase, keeping a manual forecast accurate becomes a job in itself. Here’s how software helps:

Your figures update as things happen: Where connected features are available and set up correctly, software can bring your invoices, expenses, and bank transactions into one place, so your cash position reflects more up-to-date information rather than what you entered last week.

Tax figures are easier to estimate: Rather than working out your VAT, PAYE, or corporation tax rows entirely by hand, accounting software may help you estimate, track, and organise tax-related figures from the data you enter, depending on the product, your setup, and your circumstances. You should still check these figures against HMRC guidance or with an accountant before relying on them.

Late payments are easier to spot: When an invoice goes overdue and your invoicing and bank data are kept up to date, you can more easily see how it affects your projected closing balance. For small businesses where one late payment can shift an entire month’s numbers, that early visibility can give you time to act.

Forecasting becomes part of running the business: When your data is live and connected, staying on top of your cash flow stops being a separate monthly task and becomes a natural part of how you manage day to day.

If you want to see how that works in practice, Sage Accounting brings your invoicing, expenses, banking, and tax obligations together in one place.

Frequently asked questions

			

			

	

What’s the difference between a cash flow forecast and a cash flow statement?

	

			

A cash flow forecast is forward-looking. You use it to project what you expect to come in and go out over a future period.

A cash flow statement is historical. It records what actually happened to cash in your business and forms part of your formal financial accounts.

One helps you plan ahead. The other tells you what occurred.

		

	

	

How far ahead should a cash flow forecast go?

	

			

One month gives you enough visibility to manage immediate cash needs. Three months works better for planning decisions like hiring, supplier negotiations, or upcoming tax bills.

If you’re seeking funding or managing growth, maintain a 12-month forecast and update it monthly so the window always stays a year ahead.

		

	

	

Can I use a cash flow forecast for a start-up?

	

			

Yes, and it may be the single most important financial document you produce at that stage. Map out when you expect customers to pay, what your fixed costs look like, and how long your funding will last.

Lenders and investors may ask for it, and it helps you agree on workable payment terms with clients and suppliers from the start.

Your early figures will be estimates, and that’s fine. The discipline of building and updating the forecast is what matters.

		

	

	

Do I need a cash flow forecast for a loan or funding application?

	

			

Many lenders and investors may ask for one. It shows you understand your numbers, that you’ve thought through how the funding will be used, and you have a realistic repayment plan. The free cash flow forecast template above can give you a starting point, but lenders or investors may require additional information, specific formats, or professionally prepared forecasts.

	

	

Can ChatGPT make a cash flow forecast?

	

			

LLMs like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude can generate a structure or populate a template, but they have no access to your actual business data. Unless you upload your actual numbers, any figures it produces are fabricated or based on generic assumptions with no relation to your real income or costs.

Do not upload sensitive business or customer data to any AI tool unless you are satisfied it is appropriate to do so and you understand how the tool will use, store, and protect that data.

		

	

		

	

This article was verified by a UK-based Accountant in September 2026. Accounting rules are complex and change frequently and we recommend you seek any accounting advice from a qualified accountant or tax professional. This template and guidance are for general information only and do not constitute accounting, tax, legal or financial advice. Tax obligations, payment dates and available reliefs depend on your business structure, registration status, accounting period and circumstances. Check the latest HMRC guidance or speak to a qualified accountant or tax adviser before relying on figures for tax, funding or business decisions.

title: Embedded accounting: The opportunity for accountants
snippet: As clients change how they keep their books, discover what embedded accounting means for your role and your practice. The post Embedded accounting: The opportunity for accountants appeared first on Sage Advice UK.
fullText:
More small businesses are now recording income and expenses directly in the banking and business apps they use every day.

But that doesn’t remove the need for professional accounting advice.

In fact, it can create new opportunities to support clients, particularly those who are still building confidence with digital record-keeping.

Clients still need your expertise to assess what they’ve recorded, identify what’s missing, and understand what it means for their business.

This article breaks down what embedded accounting means for your practice, how to support clients using it and take advantage of its benefits, and how Sage is helping accountants and bookkeepers stay connected to the record.

Here’s what we’ll cover:

What is embedded accounting?

Embedded accounting means accounting features are built directly into the banking, fintech, and business software platforms your clients already use.

This could look like capturing receipts, categorising transactions, or creating invoices within the same app they use to manage their money, depending on their chosen platform.

Many small businesses want to manage more of their day-to-day administration from a single platform.

Embedded accounting responds to that need by bringing record-keeping into the places where they already manage business activity.

What embedded accounting could mean for your practice?

You know how much time it takes chasing receipts or getting a clear explanation from a client about a payment they made months ago.

Embedded accounting helps clients build cleaner, digitised records from day one, giving you a better starting point for review.

Capturing information as they go also helps establish healthy digital habits, with Making Tax Digital (MTD) for Income Tax readiness built into the process from the start.

That can mean less chasing at quarter or year-end, when clients may have forgotten the details.

Being able to review those records without learning a different process for every client’s app is another big benefit.

A consistent workflow gives you new visibility into what clients have recorded and a way to address errors or missing information.

Clients can handle everyday record-keeping while you retain the professional oversight they rely on.

Embedded accounting also creates an opportunity for you to support new clients through the platforms they already use.

Small businesses can be more comfortable keeping everyday records in their existing apps but still need an accountant’s help.

You can build a relationship around the support they need now and develop it as their businesses grow.

How to support clients already using embedded accounting

Your clients may not call it “embedded accounting.” 

Instead, they may tell you they have already categorised transactions or uploaded receipts in their banking app. 

Start by asking which platform they use and how they’ve been using it.

That should give you an idea of what information is available and the support they may need.

Next, establish your access to their records.

You’ll need to agree on the appropriate permissions with your client and understand where their platform supports accountant access, or a connection to the tools you use.

Confirm what information is shared and whether amendments update the underlying client record, so you both understand how you will work together.

Then consider what the app hasn’t captured.

Has the client used other accounts or cards? Have they paid business expenses personally?

Are there cash payments? These questions help you establish whether the records reflect the wider business activity.

Reviewing the records brings it all together.

For the period you are reviewing, check that transactions are supported, categorisation is appropriate, and gaps have been addressed.

For example, a payment labelled as a business expense may need clarification about what was purchased and how it was used before you can make the correct adjustments.

Set a regular cadence for resolving queries with your client.

Get clear about responsibilities for supplying information, reviewing entries, and handling submission to keep the work moving throughout the year.

How Sage keeps accountants connected to the record

Sage’s role in the embedded accounting evolution is to connect the place your embedded accounting clients keep their records with the tools you use to support them. 

Sage for Accountants’ Period Review capability provides accountants with a single, unified workflow for reviewing client data and preparing records before filing.

It connects your review work to the records your client maintains in their connected partner app.

You can search, sort, and update records in bulk within one consistent review experience, whether records come from Sage ledgers or Sage’s embedded accounting partner apps.

Supported by Sage-backed accounting standards, this helps you improve data quality throughout the year and build confidence that records are ready for submission.

Even if you don’t use the full version of Sage for Accountants today, you can still support clients using embedded accounting and plug directly into their activity.

Sage’s Period Review is now available for free within the software.

You can leverage the same visibility, review, and correct records with speed, all without learning a new workflow or app for every client. Sage Period Review for Accountants was built for accountants, by accountants.

The connection and functionality available will vary depending on the platform your client uses.

You can access Period Review through Sage for Accountants.

Get started today

If your practice isn’t already using Sage for Accountants, it’s easy to sign up and get started, so you can start making Period Review part of the way you work.

A new start to a deeper connection

Embedded accounting allows your clients to keep the freedom of choosing the products that suit them without changing where they start.

Sage for Accountants keeps you connected to their records, so you can support them as their business develops.

And there will be opportunities to do more.

 Future integrations will mean more tools and capabilities as Sage continues to partner with more of the platforms your current and potential clients use to manage their money.

title: MTD for Income Tax: What accountants and clients need to do
snippet: Making Tax Digital for Income Tax has started. Here's what accountants need to know about thresholds, deadlines, and software so they can support their clients. The post MTD for Income Tax: What accountants and clients need to do appeared first on Sage Advice UK.
fullText:
Making Tax Digital (MTD) for Income Tax is the HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) requirement for sole traders and landlords within scope to keep digital records, send quarterly updates to HMRC, and file their annual Self Assessment tax return, all using MTD-compatible software. It started on 6 April 2026 for those with qualifying income above £50,000.

Key takeaways

MTD for Income Tax applies in phases: sole traders and landlords with qualifying gross income above £50,000 from April 2026, above £30,000 from April 2027, and above £20,000 from April 2028.

Only self-employment and property income counts towards the threshold—other income, such as savings interest, is ignored.

Clients within scope must keep digital records, send quarterly updates, and file their annual Self Assessment tax return by 31 January, all using MTD-compatible software.

Quarterly updates are cumulative (year to date) and are due by 7 August, 7 November, 7 February, and 7 May, and no tax is paid when an update is sent.

As the client’s main agent, you can submit the annual return once your client has reviewed it and confirmed in writing that it’s correct and complete. Quarterly updates can be submitted by you, a supporting agent such as their bookkeeper, or the client.

There can be few accountants and bookkeepers who haven’t heard of MTD for Income Tax. With the first introduction date of April 2026 now passed, you might still have work to do to get your practice ready.

This article can help. Read on to learn how you can get to grips with MTD for Income Tax across everything you do, regardless of the size of your practice or the nature of your clients.

Are you a sole trader or landlord looking for MTD for Income Tax guidance? Get our dedicated guide, written by experts.

Here’s what this article discusses:

What is Making Tax Digital for Income Tax?

MTD for Income Tax is a new way for sole traders and landlords to record and report their income to HMRC. The government has said MTD for Income Tax is being mandated in at least three phases.

It affects sole traders and landlords (or individuals who are both) that have gross income above £50,000 from April 2026, above £30,000 from April 2027, and above £20,000 from April 2028.

As happened with MTD for VAT, clients will turn to accountants for advice and guidance. 

More than this, the government is again likely relying at least partially on accountants to educate their clients about the requirements and ongoing process adaptations.

It’s vital to realise how Making Tax Digital for Income Tax provides opportunities:

Clients can modernise their accounting processes, to get the benefits of massively reduced admin and a closer, more active relationship with their accountant. Considering AI productivity assistants are now within accounting software, the improvements could be revolutionary—and not as technically onerous compared to the old days.

Accountants have an opportunity to grow their services via increased client touchpoints through quarterly updates and the digital tax return—not to mention initial guidance on signing up, adjusting admin processes, and helping with software choices. Better and accurate visibility into client data can inspire a vast range of services.

If your practice has income tax clients that fall under the scope of MTD for Income Tax, you need to start putting plans into practice today, if you haven’t already. The scale of clients impacted, which is significantly higher than for VAT a few years ago, means the quantity of work cannot be underestimated.

When does MTD for Income Tax start for my client’s business?

Your client’s MTD for Income Tax start date depends on their qualifying gross income from self-employment and property:

MTD for Income Tax start date

Qualifying gross income

Based on income in tax year

6 April 2026

Above £50,000

2024/25

6 April 2027

Above £30,000

2025/26

6 April 2028

Above £20,000

2026/27

MTD for Income Tax applies from 6 April of the relevant tax year: 6 April 2026 if qualifying income from self-employment and property on the 2024/25 return was above £50,000, 6 April 2027 if it was above £30,000 on the 2025/26 return, and 6 April 2028 if it was above £20,000 on the 2026/27 return. Your client must keep digital records from that 6 April, and their quarterly update periods follow the tax year (or calendar quarters, if they choose), whatever their accounting date.

HMRC will inform clients in writing if they need to use MTD for Income Tax.

From September 2026, HMRC is also signing up sole traders and landlords who are required to use MTD for Income Tax but haven’t registered. Find out more in HMRC-led sign-up for MTD for Income Tax: What accountants need to know.

For accounting periods before their MTD start date, those within scope will continue to use the Self Assessment system for the business.

For example, a client who started MTD for Income Tax on 6 April 2026 still files their 2025/26 Self Assessment return in the usual way by 31 January 2027 (or by 30 December 2026 if they want HMRC to collect tax through their PAYE tax code, where eligible). From 2026/27 onwards, their annual Self Assessment return is filed through compatible software.

Individuals outside the scope of MTD for Income Tax may still need to file a Self Assessment return in the usual way. Being below the MTD threshold, being a company director, or receiving pension income doesn’t on its own mean someone must file, so check HMRC’s Self Assessment filing criteria for each client.

Which clients will be affected by MTD for Income Tax and how?

To fall under the MTD for Income Tax scope, all of the £50,000/£30,000/£20,000+ income will have to come from either sole trade businesses, or property rents, or a combination of both. No other income matters for this calculation. 

For example:

For example, should one of your clients have just £49,000 from property rental to declare for income tax, and £2,000 from savings interest income, that won’t require them to sign up for MTD for Income Tax. All of this is before allowable expenses, of course.

But if they had £45,000 from sole trade income and £10,000 from property rental income, then their gross income will be £55,000—pushing them above the threshold of the April 2026 rollout, for example. HMRC bases their decision for this based on the gross income for the 2024/25 tax year, as shown on the Self Assessment tax return.

Care needs to be taken, however, because for some clients, 2024/25 may have had an unusually long basis period because of basis period reform (BPR) measures. Therefore, their earnings might be artificially high. If you believe this is the case for your client, and that their income is typically below the threshold, contact HMRC to discuss the issue.

Those new to a sole trader or property rental will use the Self Assessment system, and never go straight to using MTD for Income Tax, even if it’s clear their income will rise above £50,000 (or £30,000/£20,000 as of 2027/2028). 

Effectively, this means these clients will always complete two years of Self Assessment prior to moving to MTD for Income Tax, unless they opt to voluntarily do sign-up. This can be done even if their earnings are below the threshold. If this option is chosen, the client will complete a single year’s Self Assessment before moving to MTD for Income Tax at the start of the subsequent tax year.

What are MTD for Income Tax quarterly updates and the digital tax return?

Quarterly updates are cumulative summaries of income and expenses sent to HMRC during the year, and the annual tax return is the Self Assessment return, which clients in MTD file through compatible software.

MTD for Income Tax doesn’t abolish Self Assessment. Clients signed up to MTD still file one annual Self Assessment tax return for each tax year, but they submit it through compatible software rather than HMRC’s online service or a paper SA100.

In addition, they send quarterly updates using compatible software, as follows, and file the annual return by 31 January.

Here are the MTD for Income Tax requirements in brief:

Digital records for MTD for Income Tax

A digital record is a line item of income or expense, which is to say, each transaction. The minimum data that needs to be recorded is as follows:

Amount.

Date.

The tax category, as defined by HMRC, such as turnover, cost of goods bought for resale, or wages, salaries and other staff costs. Car, van and travel expenses are also categorised. 

Obviously, MTD-compatible accounting software will make it easy to record these details via automation.

None of this is outside the scope of data already recorded for Self Assessment, of course. The difference is simply that it must be recorded ASAP, and certainly prior to any quarterly update submission. 

Quarterly updates for MTD for Income Tax

Quarterly update deadlines are the same every year:

Quarterly update

Period ending

Latest submission date

First update

5 July

7 August

Second update

5 October

7 November

Third update

5 January

7 February

Fourth update

5 April

7 May

These are generated in MTD-compatible software by you or the client. You or their bookkeeper can submit them on behalf of the client.

Each update gives cumulative year-to-date totals for each income and expense category, from the start of the tax year to the end of the latest period. HMRC does not require individual income or expenditure records at this point, or for the tax return.

The deadlines in the table apply even if the client uses the fiscal year (1 April to 31 March) for their basis period.

An update doesn’t include any obligation or statement that the data is complete and accurate, and no tax is paid at that point.

If something in an earlier period was wrong, correct it in the digital records. The correction then flows through in the next cumulative update (or in the annual return, after the final update).

HMRC returns a calculation of the estimated tax liability based on the information sent. This should be discussed with clients, with potential inaccuracies notified (pending later adjustments).

For a step-by-step process, read MTD quarterly updates: A practice guide for accountants and bookkeepers. To understand what happens if an update is late, see Making Tax Digital for Income Tax penalties: HMRC’s new systems explained and the MTD for Income Tax penalty delay (soft landing period) explained.

Digital tax return for MTD for Income Tax

Very similar to Self Assessment, the tax return is to be completed and submitted via MTD-compatible software at the end of the tax period or any point after this date and up to the following 31 January.

A separate Business Source Adjustable Summary (BSAS) can be requested from HMRC, via the MTD-compatible software, for each business and property income. This is the foundation used by accountants to make adjustments for each income source, such as capital allowances, private use adjustments, corrections, and disallowable expenses. Accountants should not simply use the fourth quarterly update as the numbers for the tax return. BSAS totals are not a substitute for completing the digital tax return and accountants must make adjustments as required.

Remember that the MTD rules mean any adjustments/corrections must be undertaken in MTD-compatible software and legally-compliant digital links must be used between software and systems if data is transferred (e.g. from a spreadsheet to accounting software—it is not legally possible to cut/copy and paste data). 

The submission is a declaration that the information is complete and correct. The client must review and sign. As with Self Assessment, you are unable to do this for them.

Once submitted, HMRC returns a tax calculation.

The digital tax return effectively replaces the SA100 tax return. Additionally:

31 January continues to be the deadline for filing.

Any income tax liability must also be paid by 31 January (payments on account will continue).

HMRC will not provide any submission interface to allow filing without the need for software. In other words, MTD-compatible software must be used all the way through. If more than one piece of software or system is used, it must be digitally linked in a legally-compliant way.

If any information that needs to be included in the final declaration isn’t supported via software submission, then the client will also need to complete a Self Assessment tax return.

However, if data cannot be submitted digitally for whatever reason, then a SA100 may still be required. 

Supplementary forms for income tax like SA102, SA105 and so forth, are no longer required because of the use of quarterly updates to provide the data or the fact the software is connected to HMRC, so can automatically pull in detais like employment income. 

What information will clients submit for MTD for Income Tax?

Clients submit income, expenses, allowances, and adjustments for each self-employment and property business, plus other income, such as dividends and savings interest, in the tax return.

The following lists aren’t exhaustive, so check HMRC’s guidance for the full requirements.

The following are non-exhaustive lists and subject to change and confirmation by HMRC.

For a self-employment business, the data required includes:

Business income (e.g. turnover)

Business expenses (total and disallowable by type of expense, such as travel costs)

Tax allowances for vehicles and equipment (e.g. capital allowances)

Adjustments (e.g. basis adjustment)

Balancing charges

Goods and services for client’s own use.

For a property business, the data required includes:

UK and foreign property business income

UK and foreign property business expenses (e.g. premises running costs)

Allowances for property (e.g. annual investment allowance)

Adjustments on property letting (e.g. loss brought forward)

Balancing charges.

For the tax return, the individual must also include the following, among other things:

Total UK dividend income for a tax year

Taxed UK savings interest

Untaxed UK savings interest

Other income sources

Any claims or elections.

Can clients opt out of MTD for Income Tax?

As with MTD for VAT, it won’t be possible for most clients to opt out of MTD for Income Tax if they fall within its scope.

However, if they joined voluntarily in the public beta, they can opt out.

And that’s also the case if they’re in specific categories that are automatically exempt, including:

Trustees

Personal representatives

Foster carers

Those without a National Insurance number in the January before the start of the tax year.

Non-resident companies.

Those who fall under the digital exclusion rules as defined by MTD for VAT will automatically be exempted from MTD for Income Tax (although there will be no harm in checking this!).

This includes people whose disabilities mean they can’t use software, for example, for people whose remote location means internet access is impossible.

Additionally, your clients will be exempt from Making Tax Digital if their qualifying income falls below the threshold for three consecutive tax years (bearing in mind this threshold will fall each year after 2026, until reaching £20,000 for 2028/29.

Clients will require MTD-compatible software of some kind. Understandably, they may look for free solutions. Sage Sole Trader is a great example, and can help clients with simple tax affairs manage their finances with software that makes bookkeeping, transaction tracking, and both MTD for Income Tax and Self Assessment easy.

However, as an accounting professional, you will require them to have more sophisticated software if you intend to collaborate with them for quarterly updates and the tax return. There are a variety of Sage Accounting plans to meet both yours and your client needs, and will grow in features as they grow, too. Examples include VAT accounting and payroll. You can access more information on our MTD for accountants hub page.

A Sage for Accountants plan offers the chance to upsell Sage Accounting directly to clients, and comes with a host of free software for accountants, such as Final Accounts and Tax, Client Management, plus free AutoEntry, GoProposal and Futrli credits each month.

Most of the big-name cloud accounting software has already been updated for MTD for Income Tax, although this might not necessarily be true for desktop accounting software. You or your clients may need to consult the software vendor to ensure updates and patches are installed.

Older software packages that are no longer supported may not be updated, so might require the client migrate their accounting to a different package.

It will be possible to use spreadsheets for MTD for Income Tax accounting through the use of either bridging software, or special spreadsheets/worksheets that facilitate digital linking with cloud services.

Remember that the digital linking rules say that copying and pasting of MTD accounting records is not allowed, and all transfer of MTD for Income Tax data must be both digital and automated.

Because of this and other issues, using a spreadsheet is unlikely to be the most user-friendly solution.

Additionally, MTD-compatible software must be able to:

Create and store digital records

Send quarterly updates

Submit the final declaration

Receive information from HMRC.

What is digital linking for MTD for Income Tax?

Digital linking means relevant tax data must follow a fully digital path once it has entered the system. You may recall the digital linking rules from the implementation of MTD for VAT.

In summary, it aims to legally enforce a fully digital path for relevant tax data once it has entered the system. 

For example, once an expense record is entered into accounting software, that value cannot then be copied into a spreadsheet for further processing, before being pasted back. The expense record must be transferred digitally by the software, via the cloud, for example. 

There’s less of a focus on digital linking in MTD for Income Tax because there are likely to be fewer interconnected applications or systems compared to VAT. But it still applies if spreadsheets are in use, as a key example, and could impact retail clients who use electronic point of sale (EPOS) systems with accounting software, or who use online auction software. 

In such a case, the two (or more) systems must be digitally linked in a legally compliant way, typically by sharing data in the cloud (e.g. the EPOS system will be available as an add-in extension for the accounting software, via the accounting software’s App Store).

Furthermore, if you work with clients then you’ll need to ensure data transfer happens digitally (although emailing and transferring files via a USB memory stick are acceptable). 

Do clients signed up for MTD for VAT need to sign up for MTD for Income Tax?

Not automatically. Clients signed up for MTD for VAT only need to sign up for MTD for Income Tax if they meet its own criteria. The two Making Tax Digital schemes for VAT and Income Tax operate independently, with their own sign up criteria.

It isn’t the case that MTD for Income Tax applies only to those already using MTD for VAT—although many businesses already using MTD for VAT will find themselves having to sign up for MTD for Income Tax too.

What are the MTD for Income Tax easements for clients?

HMRC has provided easements for joint property owners, businesses using three-line accounts, and retail businesses recording daily takings. Following feedback, HMRC has provided a handful of easements to assist certain kinds of businesses:

Joint property ownership

A joint owner of a property only needs to submit their own share of income and expenses (e.g. one record for each), and not the full figures for the property. 

They will need to provide records for total rent, other income from the property, premiums for the grant of a lease, and reverse premiums and inducements. For expenses, records should include property repairs and maintenance, residential finance costs, professional fees, and more (for more details, see sections 2.1 and 2.2 of HMRC’s MTD for Income Tax Update Notice).

Each joint owner will need to separately and independently follow the MTD for Income Tax rules, however, such as using MTD-compatible software. Furthermore, legally-compliant digital linking is required between applications and systems. Landlords who use spreadsheets to track depreciation of assets cannot copy and paste data into their accounting software, for example. In situations like this, use of professional MTD-compatible property management software is advisable. 

Three-line accounts

Already possible for Self Assessment, this easement can also be used for MTD for Income Tax. 

Clients with an annual turnover below the VAT registration threshold (currently £90,000) may opt to submit total income and expenses rather than breaking these figures down by tax category.

However, given the requirement to keep digital records of income and expenditure in any event, and the use of MTD-compatible software that will automatically produce detailed quarterly updates and a tax return based on those records, it’s unclear how useful this easement will be.

Retail sales

Clients may choose to record the daily gross takings for all retail sales as a single digital record. This must include all payments from cash paying customers, plus credit sales, gift card redemptions, sales competed via third-party booking platforms, and so on. For more details, see section 3 of HMRC’s MTD for Income Tax Digital Record Keeping Notice.

What does MTD for Income Tax mean for accountants?

MTD for Income Tax means more frequent client contact, a bigger role in software choices, and new opportunities for advisory work. It’s hard to overstate the changes it will bring for you.

Here are two things to be aware of:

1. Your clients will have to use software

Your clients will be required to use compatible software to record their business and property income and expenditure and send five updates/reports every year to HMRC.

There’s likely to be automation for each of these steps, minimising the administrative impact. But your clients still need to be aware of the requirements expected of them.

This will require a substantial change in attitude from your clients in how they approach their accounting.

It’s certainly the case that the “shoebox” client who dumps receipts on their accountant’s desk in January each year will have to change their ways.

It’s your role to communicate this need for change, and to encourage it to happen.

In return, you’ re given significant privilege to guide your clients towards the best solution for their needs—and to bring positive changes to their clients’ businesses.

This presents additional opportunities.

Not partnering with a software vendor to sell solutions to your clients, for example, is to discard a potentially large income source.

Needless to say, an MTD for Income Tax-compatible cloud accounting solution that ties into your own systems is best for both you and your client.

You can offer training in the software, perhaps as part of the sales package, or as a separate service offering.

At the very least, every UK accountant will need to be proficient in the MTD-compatible software their clients use, because accountants will be facing client enquiries about this on a very regular basis.

2. You have the opportunity to offer additional advisory services

Although MTD for Income Tax should mean clients are more aware of their accounting, it doesn’t mean your fundamental role will change.

You’ll still be required to help your clients be compliant, and to support them with fundamentals such as making deductions and calculating a final income tax bill.

While it’s possible some small business owners may have an epiphany moment when they get to grips with accounting software and realise the power it delivers, the fundamental fact that many people hate dealing with figures and the ensuing admin burden isn’t going to change.

You have nothing to fear from technology and, in fact, lots to gain.

But this is only scratching the surface of the potential that MTD for Income Tax will deliver.

You’ll go from having a single point of contact each year to potentially having at least five situations where your clients may need help with their accounting when they make those quarterly reports and the final declaration.

These situations can be used to forge stronger relationships where you’re not viewed as just a number cruncher but more of a business partner.

Using cloud software that ties in with your clients’ accounting gives you the ability to monitor for problems or opportunities, and to provide advice based on this.

For ideas on how to package and price this ongoing work, read Pricing for MTD: How to charge more, and prove it’s worth it.

Final thoughts on MTD for Income Tax

If your practice dealt with the implementation of MTD for VAT ahead of it being mandated in April 2019, you’ll be well aware that starting early with preparations will put you and your clients in good stead.

If it didn’t, the best advice is to start now.

Look at your processes, start talking to your clients, and take the steps now to not only meet the requirements for MTD for Income Tax but to use it as an opportunity to help your practice and your clients really flourish.

MTD for Income Tax for accountants: FAQs

			

			

	

Who has to use MTD for Income Tax?

	

			

Sole traders and landlords with qualifying gross income above £50,000 from April 2026, above £30,000 from April 2027, and above £20,000 from April 2028. Only income from self-employment and property counts towards the threshold.

	

	

When are MTD for Income Tax quarterly updates due?

	

			

Quarterly updates give cumulative year-to-date figures and must be sent by 7 August, 7 November, 7 February, and 7 May, covering the quarters ending 5 July, 5 October, 5 January, and 5 April. No tax is paid when an update is sent.

	

	

Do clients still need to file a Self Assessment tax return?

	

			

Yes. MTD for Income Tax doesn’t abolish Self Assessment. Clients starting in April 2026 file their 2025/26 return in the usual way by 31 January 2027. From 2026/27, they still file one annual Self Assessment return, but through compatible software.

	

	

Can an accountant submit the digital tax return for a client?

	

			

Yes, if you’re the client’s main agent. You must check the calculation, share the return with your client for review, and get their written confirmation that it’s correct and complete before you submit it through compatible software. Supporting agents, such as a bookkeeper, can submit quarterly updates but not the annual return.

	

	

Can clients use spreadsheets for MTD for Income Tax?

	

			

Yes, clients can use spreadsheets, but only with bridging software or spreadsheets that facilitate digital linking with cloud services. Copying and pasting MTD accounting records isn’t allowed, but a spreadsheet used with compatible bridging software is a valid option.

fullText:
Key takeaways

MTD for Income Tax is live. It became law for sole traders and landlords with qualifying income over £50,000 on 6 April 2026.

It’s had a difficult history since its inception in 2015, with several postponements and rescoping of who/what is included. But that’s all history now. 

The £30,000 threshold applies from 6 April 2027. The £20,000 threshold applies from 6 April 2028.

No penalty points for late quarterly updates in 2026/27. From 2027/28, each missed deadline earns a point, with a £200 penalty at four.

It’s a fair question. Making Tax Digital (MTD) for Income Tax was first pencilled in for 2018, then 2023, then 2024, before landing on April 2026.

The good news? That pattern is now broken and MTD is steaming ahead. Any further cancellations or postponements are very unlikely. 

The first wave is in, covering incomes over £50,000 and, at the time of publication, the first quarterly updates have been filed.

What’s more, HMRC is actively signing up people who haven’t done so themselves. 

The question isn’t “will it happen” any more. It’s “which date applies to me, and am I ready for it?”.

Let’s take a closer look, as follows:

Is MTD delayed in 2026/2027/2028? The short answer is…

No. 

GOV.UK confirms that if your qualifying income was over £50,000 in 2024/25, you should already be using MTD for Income Tax, and that if you haven’t signed up you still can.

HMRC and the UK government’s position is that MTD is now a legal requirement and that anyone in scope should check they’re signed up, their software is compatible, and their update is in before the deadline.

One thing did soften, and it’s probably feeding any rumour you may have heard: HMRC won’t apply penalty points for late quarterly updates in the 2026/27 tax year. 

That’s a soft landing on lateness, not a pause. The obligation to keep digital records and send updates stands.

The official and confirmed MTD deadlines from 2026 and 2027 onwards

HMRC publishes the full timeline on its Making Tax Digital campaign site and in the quarterly updates guidance on GOV.UK. 

For anyone already in the first wave, the next dates at the time of publication are as follows. 

Watch out for some gotchas, such as deadlines occurring over the weekend:

7 November 2026: 2nd quarterly update (covering 6 April to 5 October). Falls on a Saturday.

31 January 2027: Your 2025/26 Self Assessment return, filed the usual way.

7 February 2027: 3rd quarterly update. Falls on a Sunday.

6 April 2027: The £30,000 wave kicks off, and those included should start keeping digital records.

7 May 2027: 4th quarterly update. Falls on a Friday.

7 August 2027: First quarterly update of 2027/28, for both those included in the £50,000 wave and those included in the £30,000 wave.

31 January 2028: The first MTD tax return for 2026/27, with any required tax payment due the same day. This covers all your sources of income, unlike quarterly updates, which are limited to income and expenditure. 

A detail worth diarising: Three of the next four quarterly deadlines fall on a weekend, and January/February 2027 stacks a Self Assessment return and then an MTD quarterly update a week apart. 

If you rely on an accountant, that’s their busiest fortnight of the year, so make sure you get everything over to them well ahead of time.

Who’s affected, and when

GOV.UK’s rule is simple to state. You need MTD for Income Tax if you’re a sole trader or landlord registered for Self Assessment and your qualifying income is over the threshold for that tax year:

Over £50,000 in 2024/25: You should’ve started on 6 April 2026.

Over £30,000 in 2025/26: You start on 6 April 2027.

Over £20,000 in 2026/27: You start on 6 April 2028.

Partnerships will follow at a date HMRC hasn’t yet set. You can check your own position with HMRC’s online tool.

Will Making Tax Digital spread to other taxes?

MTD already covers VAT, and is in the process of rolling out to apply to Income Tax: sole traders and landlords earning over £50,000 join from April 2026, over £30,000 from April 2027 and over £20,000 from April 2028. 

Beyond that, HMRC has pulled back. Its July 2025 Transformation Roadmap stated: “HMRC does not intend to introduce MTD for Corporation Tax“. 

So, limited companies keep filing annual returns as now. 

HMRC is still exploring digitalisation for sole traders below £20,000, and aims to be “digital-first” by 2030 through pre-populated returns, AI tools, and possible e-invoicing.

6 lesser-known MTD details that catch people out

1. It’s turnover, not profit

The single most common question in the first quarter was still “does this apply to me?”, usually confusing profit with turnover and unsure which income sources count. 

Qualifying income is gross income from self-employment and property, combined. A side business plus a rental flat can tip you over together even if neither does alone.

2. No letter doesn’t mean no obligation

HMRC writes to people it believes are in scope, but HMRC is explicit that if you don’t receive a letter it’s still your responsibility to check and sign up, if required.

3. The £20,000 wave is a different animal

The smallest cohort will often have simpler accounts but a harder journey: lower software adoption, more “once a year in a shoebox” habits, more landlords with mixed income, and far more people with no accountant acting as translator. 

If you earn around £20,000 from a trade or a rental, the honest truth is that accounting has probably never been something you took seriously. 

From April 2028, you’ll need to. Start now, and make life easier for yourself.

4. Preparing and filing are different moments

Many people signed up and connected their software weeks early, then waited until the final days to send the update. The deadline created its own peak. 

Build a habit of sending the update as soon as the quarter closes.

5. Updates are cumulative, so mistakes should self-correct

Each update covers from 6 April to the end of the period. 

This means you can fix any data that was wrong, and the correction flows into the next update automatically. You’ve no need to specifically call anything out as a mistake.

6. Nil updates still count

If you had no income or expenses in a period, you still have to send the update.

Final thoughts

MTD for Income Tax isn’t delayed, and it’s unlikely it will be from this point onwards.

The people who had the smoothest first quarter weren’t lucky. They’d got software in place early, kept bookkeeping ticking over weekly, and set internal deadlines ahead of the statutory ones.

The 2026/27 year is the cheapest it will ever be to learn the rhythm, because lateness won’t cost penalty points. From 2027/28, it will.

Takeaway: check your 2025/26 turnover now. If it’s over £30,000, your start date is 6 April 2027 and your first deadline is 7 August 2027. If it’s over £20,000, you’ve got until April 2028, but the habits take longer to build than the software does.

MTD delays and postponement FAQs

			

			

	

Has MTD for Income Tax been delayed again in 2026?

	

			

No. It went live on 6 April 2026 for qualifying income over £50,000 and the first quarterly update deadline has already passed.

	

	

Will the £30,000 threshold be delayed?

	

			

GOV.UK currently states 6 April 2027 for qualifying income over £30,000 in 2025/26, and no change has been announced.

	

	

Does MTD change when I pay tax?

	

			

No. Your tax return and payment are still due by 31 January after the tax year ends; for 2026/27 that’s 31 January 2028. Ditto for any payments on account required by HMRC, which are also due on 31 July.

	

	

Will MTD apply to Corporation Tax?

	

			

No. HMRC originally planned for this to be the case, but has since permanently cancelled that project. 

Although Corporation Tax accounting and filing might be digitalised in other ways moving forward, at the moment it’s still built around keeping compliant accounting records and submitting a Corporation Tax return—just as it has been for decades.

		

	

	

Will MTD apply to taxes like Inheritance Tax or Capital Gains?

	

			

No. Making Tax Digital (MTD) for Income Tax applies to qualifying income from self-employment and property. HMRC confirms that other sources of income, such as employment, pensions and dividends, do not count towards the qualifying-income thresholds, although they may still need to be included in the taxpayer’s overall digital tax return on 31 January.

Capital Gains Tax (CGT) is reported through separate HMRC digital services or Self Assessment, rather than through MTD’s quarterly updates. UK residential property gains must generally be reported, and any CGT due paid, within 60 days of completion. Other taxable gains can be reported through HMRC’s real-time CGT service by 31 December in the tax year following the disposal, with payment due by 31 January, or through Self Assessment. Where a taxpayer uses MTD for Income Tax, other taxable income and gains must still be included in the annual digital tax return, normally by 31 January.

Inheritance Tax is being digitalised separately. HMRC’s Transformation Roadmap, updated in 2026, confirms plans to replace the existing paper-based process with an end-to-end digital service from the 2027/28 tax year.

		

	

	

Are any MTD quarterly updates delayed, postponed, or cancelled? 

	

			

The simple yet complete answer is no! See the body of this article for a list of deadlines. 

	

	

Is the MTD for Income Tax digital tax return delayed, postponed, or cancelled?

	

			

No. You should submit this via your MTD-ready software by 31 January. Bear in mind that, although HMRC is not enforcing penalties if you miss an MTD quarterly deadline in the first year of MTD for Income Tax (2026/27), this does not extend to the tax return deadline—they are likely to impose penalties if you miss it!
